content.value_statement: Testing esoteric language examples can be slow to set up. This skill returns a fixed greeting generated by a Brainfuck program.
actual_capabilities: Runs a packaged Brainfuck program with the beef interpreter.
Returns a fixed greeting message with no required input.
Demonstrates an Enact tool manifest with input and output schemas.
Shows Brainfuck commands and a small ASCII construction example.
Supports CLI execution and MCP agent invocation patterns.
limitations: It does not accept custom text or Brainfuck source input.
It only returns one predefined greeting message.
It depends on the beef package during container build.
It is an example skill, not a general Brainfuck development environment.

use_cases.title: Learn Esoteric Language Basics
use_cases.description: Students can inspect a small Brainfuck program that prints a readable greeting.

use_cases.title: Test Enact Tool Execution
use_cases.description: Tool authors can verify that a minimal no-input Enact skill runs through CLI or MCP.

use_cases.title: Demonstrate Agent Tool Calls
use_cases.description: AI workflow builders can use a harmless fixed-output tool to test agent integration.

prompt_templates.title: Run the Greeting
prompt_templates.prompt: Use enact-hello-brainfuck with no arguments and tell me the returned greeting.

prompt_templates.title: Explain the Output
prompt_templates.prompt: Run the skill, then explain how the Brainfuck program produces the greeting at a high level.

prompt_templates.title: Compare Invocation Modes
prompt_templates.prompt: Show how this skill can be invoked from the CLI and from an MCP agent using its documentation.

prompt_templates.title: Audit the Example Tool
prompt_templates.prompt: Review the skill manifest and Brainfuck source. Identify the fixed behavior, dependencies, and operational risks.

output_examples.input: Run the skill with no arguments.
output_examples.output: The skill returns the greeting message: Hello from Brainfuck!

output_examples.input: Ask for a summary of what the Brainfuck program does.
output_examples.output: It explains that the source prints a fixed greeting one character at a time.

output_examples.input: Ask whether custom input is supported.
output_examples.output: It states that the skill accepts no input and always returns the same greeting.

best_practices: Use the skill as a deterministic smoke test for agent tool calling.
Review the manifest dependency before running it in a restricted environment.
Pair the output with the source file when teaching Brainfuck basics.
anti_patterns: Do not treat it as a Brainfuck interpreter for arbitrary user programs.
Do not rely on it for dynamic greetings or localization.
Do not use the example output as proof that unrelated tool chains are configured correctly.

faq.question: What does this skill do?
faq.answer: It runs a packaged Brainfuck program and returns a fixed greeting.

faq.question: Does it require input?
faq.answer: No. The input schema has no properties, so the tool runs without arguments.

faq.question: Can it run my own Brainfuck code?
faq.answer: No. The included program is fixed and does not accept custom source.

faq.question: Which interpreter does it use?
faq.answer: The manifest runs the program with the beef Brainfuck interpreter.

faq.question: Can Claude, Codex, and Claude Code use it?
faq.answer: Yes. The report marks support for Claude, Codex, and Claude Code.

faq.question: Is it useful beyond a demo?
faq.answer: It is best for smoke tests, teaching examples, and simple agent integration checks.
